newsitem.title: USA: DuPont Merck drug cocktail lowers HIV - study.
newsitem.headline: DuPont Merck drug cocktail lowers HIV - study.

text.p: DuPont Merck's DMP 266 drug, used with Merck and Co Inc's Crixivan, moved the HIV-RNA, or viral load, below the quantification level in 80 percent of patients, data from an initial ongoing Phase II study showed.
These patients also achieved CD4 immune cell count elevation averaging 140 cells/mm, DuPont Merck said.

CD4 cells are key cells which HIV destroys, undermining the immune system. A low count of these cells would indicate advanced AIDS. DuPont Merck Pharmaceutical Co is a global, research-based drug company which was formed in 1991 as a partnership between Merck and DuPont Co.
Patients enrolled in the study groups had CD4 counts of 100 to 500 cells and more than 20,000 copies of HIV-RNA in the bloodstream at the time of the study, DuPont Merck said.

The combination also achieved a 99.99 percent reduction in HIV-RNA among patients studied, the company said. Findings were presented at the Eighth European Congress of Clinical Microbiology and Infectuous Diseases in Lausanne, Switzerland.
In the study, 21 patients received indinavir, or Crixivan, for two weeks, followed by combination therapy with DMP 266, a non-nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor, it said.
Additional studies using higher doses of DMP 266 with indinavir were underway, the company said.
Another group of nine patients received the protease inhibitor indinavir alone for 26 weeks, followed by the addition of Bristol-Myers Squibb Co's Zerit, or stavudine, and DMP 266, it said.

At 26 weeks, about 40 percent of the patients receiving indinavir alone had plasma levels below 400 copies/mL of HIV-RNA, it said. After stavudine and DMP 266 were added, and following 16 weeks of triple combination therapy, 83 percent of the patients had plasma levels below this point.

"DMP 266's apparent ability to significantly drop viral load in HIV-infected patients is good news," said Kenneth Wagner, associate professor of medicine in the division of infectuous diseases, Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences, Bethseda, Md.
In both study groups, DMP 266 was well-tolerated although two patients were discontinued from treatment due to an adverse clinical event, it said.
The most commonly reported side effects for the indinavir monotherapy and DMP 266-indinavir groups were rash, sinusitis, upper respitory infection and diarrhea, it said.
"In clinical trials, we are finding DMP 266 is emerging as a potent weapon in combating HIV," said Henry Pan, executive vice president of clinical development at DuPont Merck.
